custodyAssets.title: Client assets serviced
custodyAssets.content:
AUM is client assets Northern Trust actively manages (Wealth Management and asset-management mandates). Assets under custody are safekept and settled for clients without discretion. AUC/A adds administration services (fund accounting, reporting) on top of custody, so it is the broadest and largest of the three.

For Northern Trust Corporation: fee revenue in Asset Servicing scales with AUC/A and custody balances, while Wealth Management fees scale with AUM -- both move with markets as well as net new business, so a quarter's growth is not all organic.

What to watch:

  • AUC/A and custody growing faster than markets (net new business) versus just riding a rally
  • AUM growth versus Wealth Management segment revenue growth (fee-rate compression)

capitalRatio.title: CET1 capital ratio
capitalRatio.content:
CET1 (Common Equity Tier 1) ratio is core regulatory capital divided by risk-weighted assets -- the primary measure regulators and the Fed's stress tests use to judge a bank's loss-absorbing buffer.

For Northern Trust Corporation: as a systemically important custody bank, NTRS targets a buffer above the ~7% regulatory minimum (plus its own surcharge); the ratio also gates how much it can return via buybacks and dividends.

What to watch:

  • Ratio trending down toward the regulatory minimum plus buffer
  • Buybacks accelerating when the ratio is well above target, pausing when it is not

roe.title: Return on equity
roe.content:
ROE is net income divided by average shareholders' equity -- the standard profitability yardstick for a bank, where equity (not invested capital) is the scarce resource.

For Northern Trust Corporation: ROE here is quarterly and can swing with one-off items (e.g. the Visa share gain), so compare FY figures or several quarters, not a single print.

What to watch:

  • ROE trend versus cost of equity
  • Single-quarter spikes or drops driven by non-recurring items

segments.title: Business segments
segments.content:
Northern Trust reports two segments: Asset Servicing (custody, fund administration, securities lending for institutions) and Wealth Management (trust, banking and investment services for individuals and families).

For Northern Trust Corporation: Asset Servicing is the larger, more scale- and rate-sensitive segment; Wealth Management typically carries the higher margin. The split shows which engine is driving growth and which is driving profitability.

What to watch:

  • Operating margin (operating income / revenue) diverging between the two segments
  • Which segment is driving revenue growth versus which is driving profit growth

funding.title: Deposits and net interest income
funding.content:
Deposits are the low-cost funding Northern Trust takes in alongside custody relationships; net interest income is what it earns investing them less what it pays depositors and other funding.

For Northern Trust Corporation: client deposits (often non-interest-bearing operating balances tied to custody) are a byproduct of the custody business, not a separate retail franchise -- so deposits can swing with client cash balances, not just rate-driven competition for funding.

What to watch:

  • NII moving with the rate cycle even when deposit balances are flat
  • Deposit balances falling as clients shift idle cash into higher-yielding alternatives

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Northern Trust Corporation: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Northern Trust Corporation: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Northern Trust Corporation: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Northern Trust Corporation: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Northern Trust Corporation: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

nim.title: Net interest margin
nim.content:
NIM is net interest income as a percentage of interest-earning assets.

For Northern Trust Corporation: the core profitability metric of a lender; a few basis points move earnings materially.

What to watch:

  • NIM trend with the rate cycle
  • Funding cost versus lending yield

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Northern Trust Corporation: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Northern Trust Corporation: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Northern Trust Corporation: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Northern Trust Corporation: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
